title: Former “We Buy Ugly Houses” Franchisee Sentenced to Federal Prison for $3M Fraud Scheme—DOJ Announces
body:
A federal judge on Thursday ordered Charles Carrier, the former president of a Dallas‑based investment firm and a disgraced franchisee of the HomeVestors “We Buy Ugly Houses” network, to serve a prison term for orchestrating a multi‑million‑dollar fraud scheme that preyed on distressed homeowners and investors alike. Carrier received a sentence of 33 months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release and a restitution order exceeding $4 million, underscoring the Department of Justice’s resolve to crack down on deceptive practices in the real‑estate “fix‑and‑flip” industry.

The fraud unfolded between 2018 and 2022, when Carrier, leveraging his former role as a franchisee, misrepresented the value of properties he purchased from homeowners facing financial hardship. He routinely inflated appraisal figures, falsified repair estimates, and then resold the homes at artificially high prices to investors within his own network. In several instances, the properties were sold without completing the promised renovations, leaving buyers with costly, unfinished projects. The scheme also involved a parallel money‑laundering operation in which Carrier funneled proceeds through a series of shell companies to obscure the illicit origin of the funds.

Prosecutors highlighted that Carrier’s actions violated multiple statutes, including wire fraud, bank fraud, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The Department of Justice’s fraud division noted that the scheme generated roughly $5.2 million in illicit gains, with victims ranging from low‑income homeowners who were pressured into quick sales to seasoned real‑estate investors who suffered significant losses. In addition to the prison term, Carrier was ordered to forfeit a luxury vehicle and several bank accounts, and to pay $4.2 million in restitution to the victims.

Legal experts say the case is emblematic of broader vulnerabilities within the fast‑growing “we buy houses” franchise model, which promises rapid cash offers to homeowners in distress. While the franchise system is designed to provide standardized practices and oversight, the decentralized nature of individual franchisees can create gaps that unscrupulous operators exploit. “The HomeVestors brand has a reputation for speed and convenience, but that very speed can be weaponized by bad actors who bypass due diligence,” said Laura Mendoza, a professor of real‑estate law at the University of Texas at Austin. “Regulators and franchisors must tighten compliance protocols, including more rigorous background checks and mandatory third‑party appraisals, to protect both consumers and investors.”

The HomeVestors corporate office issued a statement distancing itself from Carrier’s conduct, emphasizing that franchisees operate as independent businesses and that the company has zero tolerance for fraudulent activity. The company announced plans to enhance its monitoring systems, including real‑time auditing of transaction data and mandatory ethics training for all franchisees. Industry watchdogs have welcomed these steps but warn that systemic reforms are needed to curb a pattern of abuse that has surfaced in other regions, where similar “cash‑for‑homes” schemes have been linked to inflated valuations and undisclosed repair shortcuts.

Looking ahead, the sentencing sends a clear warning to other participants in the distressed‑property market that deceptive practices will be met with severe legal consequences. Federal authorities have indicated that investigations into related schemes are ongoing, and they have urged victims to come forward with information. As the real‑estate sector continues to grapple with the fallout from the pandemic‑induced housing crunch, tighter enforcement and more transparent franchise operations may become essential to restoring consumer confidence and safeguarding the integrity of the market.
